# Streaming, Worked Out

Source: https://pasekpasek.github.io/streaming-worked-out/
Author: Paweł Pasek
Verified against: a real node:http server and a real fetch + ReadableStream client (SSE parsing),
the real TextDecoder (UTF-8 chunk boundaries), and executed matrices for the two resumption designs.
RFC, spec and MDN statements are quoted from those documents.

A server writes. Some time later, a browser has words on it. In between sit a transfer coding, a
framing rule and a decoder, and every bug in a streaming feature lives in one of those three. This is
the plain-text version of the page, without the sandboxes.

## 01. Three things always true about a stream

Streaming looks like a feature you add. It is closer to a constraint you accept: the moment a
response stops arriving all at once, three things become true and stay true, whether the payload is
log lines, stock ticks or a model's tokens.

1. The pieces are not yours to choose. One write() on the server is not one read() on the client.
   The TCP stack, the proxies in between and the client's buffer all get a vote on where the
   boundaries fall. Code that assumes "one write, one message" works perfectly on localhost and fails
   the first time a payload crosses an MTU or a proxy coalesces two writes.
2. Therefore a stream needs a framing rule — something that says "this unit is complete." Without one
   you cannot distinguish "nothing more yet" from "nothing more ever". SSE's rule is a blank line;
   the Anthropic Messages API's is content_block_stop; other protocols prefix each frame with its
   length. The rule differs, the need for one does not.
3. A stream can stop in the middle, and resuming needs somebody to have remembered a position. The
   sender cannot know what arrived — that is the one thing it has no access to. Only the receiver
   knows what it saw, so the receiver has to say so on the way back in. That is the entire reason the
   Last-Event-ID header exists.

Everything below is one of those three wearing a costume. A data: field held in a buffer is fact 1;
a blank line is fact 2; a retry: value and a reconnect header are fact 3. So is a model's tool call
arriving as JSON that is not valid JSON yet.

## 02. An HTTP response that doesn't end

Before any streaming-specific machinery, the server must be allowed to keep writing to a response it
has already started. That is not a trick played on HTTP; it is a transfer coding, specified.

An ordinary response announces its size up front with Content-Length, which a server can only do if
it already knows the size — which it does not, if the content is still being produced. RFC 9112
states the alternative's purpose exactly: "Chunked enables content streams of unknown size to be
transferred as a sequence of length-delimited buffers, which enables the sender to retain connection
persistence and the recipient to know when it has received the entire message." The coding "is
complete when a chunk with a chunk-size of zero is received" — so a streaming endpoint simply never
sends that terminating chunk.

    res.writeHead(200, {
      'content-type': 'text/event-stream',
      'cache-control': 'no-cache',
      connection: 'keep-alive',
    })
    res.flushHeaders()   // send the headers NOW, don't wait for the first body write

    res.write('data: first\n\n')   // ...and the response stays open

flushHeaders() is the one people miss. Without it Node may hold the headers until it has body bytes
worth sending, so a client waiting for a response waits for your first event instead of for the
connection. On a slow first token — which is every model call — that is the difference between
"instant" and "broken".

Note what is not here: no protocol upgrade, no handshake, no second port. This is a plain GET that
has not finished, which is why SSE works through anything that speaks HTTP — and why, in §09,
anything that speaks HTTP a little too enthusiastically can break it.

Source: RFC 9112 §7.1, https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9112#section-7.1

## 03. SSE: the wire format

Given a response that stays open, SSE answers "where does one message end?" The answer is a
blank line.

SSE in one paragraph: Server-Sent Events is a text format for the body of an HTTP response that stays
open. The server writes plain text following a few rules, and the client cuts that text into separate
messages called events. There's no new protocol and no server library. Sending an event is a
res.write() of a string. Data only flows one way, from server to client. The same spec also defines
EventSource, the browser's built-in SSE client (§04). You don't have to use it: any code that reads
the response and cuts on the same rule is an SSE client too (§07). Every AI chat UI works this way.

The blank line is two newline characters. This is the whole server side of sending one event:

    res.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify({ text: "The" })}\n\n`)

The string ends with two \n bytes (0x0A). The first ends the line `data: {"text":"The"}`. The second
ends a line with nothing on it, the "blank line", and that is the signal that the event is complete.
So there are two levels: one \n ends a line (one field), and an empty line ends the whole event. You
need both because an event can have several lines (⏎ = \n):

    id: 42⏎
    event: task.completed⏎
    data: {"taskId":"write-intro","actor":"writer"}⏎
    ⏎                         <- empty line: event #1 is complete
    data: a plain message with no id or type⏎
    ⏎                         <- event #2, dispatched as the generic "message"

Why a separator is needed at all: the server always puts \n\n right after a complete event, but the
client doesn't receive events, it receives bytes. Each read() returns whatever has arrived so far,
and those pieces don't line up with the server's writes:

    the server wrote two events, each complete and ending in \n\n
    write() #1   data: {"text":"The"}\n\n
    write() #2   data: {"text":" cat"}\n\n

    the client got exactly the same bytes, cut in different places
    read()  #1   data: {"text":"The"}\n\ndata: {"te
    read()  #2   xt":" cat"}\n\n

The \n\n in the middle of read #1 is not in the middle of an object. It is the end of event #1,
where the server put it. What follows is the start of event #2, whose rest only arrives in read #2.

A client that is even slightly busy sees this all the time. In a real run where the client did
something else for 300 ms, three separate writes (50 ms apart) arrived as one read:

    write()  "data: {\"text\":\"The\"}\n\n"
    write()  "data: {\"text\":\" cat\"}\n\n"
    write()  "data: {\"text\":\" sat\"}\n\n"
    read()   "data: {\"text\":\"The\"}\n\ndata: {\"text\":\" cat\"}\n\ndata: {\"text\":\" sat\"}\n\n"

The client keeps a buffer and cuts it on \n\n:

    buffer += chunk
    const events = buffer.split("\n\n")
    buffer = events.pop()               // the last piece may be unfinished: keep it for later
    for (const ev of events) show(ev)   // everything else is a complete event

Traced through the two reads above:

    read #1: buffer = 'data: {"text":"The"}\n\ndata: {"te'
             split  -> ['data: {"text":"The"}', 'data: {"te']   show event #1, keep 'data: {"te'
    read #2: buffer = 'data: {"te' + 'xt":" cat"}\n\n' = 'data: {"text":" cat"}\n\n'
             split  -> ['data: {"text":" cat"}', '']         show event #2, keep ''

Without the separator, `data: {"te` at the end of read #1 would look like a whole message and
JSON.parse would throw on it.

A real parser goes line by line instead, because it also has to handle \r\n, comments and multiple
data: lines. The rule is the same. On the wire, curl -N shows the blank lines as gaps, and
`curl -N ... | cat -A` shows every \n as $:

    data: {"text":"The"}$
    $
    data: {"text":" cat"}$
    $

The fields:

    id: 42
- data: — the payload. Several data: lines before the blank line join with newlines into one event's
  data, which is how multi-line content travels without an escape.
- event: — the type a client filters on with addEventListener(type, ...). Omit it and the event
  dispatches as the generic "message".
- id: — the resumption checkpoint; the client remembers the last one it saw.
- retry: — how many milliseconds to wait before reconnecting. Per the spec, if the value "consists of
  only ASCII digits" it is interpreted as an integer and sets "the event stream's reconnection time".
- A line starting with ":" is a comment and is ignored. Servers send these as keep-alives so idle
  connections are not reaped (§09).

Two spec details cause real bugs. On the colon: "Collect the characters on the line before the first
U+003A COLON character (:), and let field be that string" — the field name is everything before the
FIRST colon, so a JSON payload full of colons is safe on a data: line. And on the terminator: "Note
that the last still has to end with a blank line, the end of the stream is not enough to trigger the
dispatch of the last event."

Read that twice if you are writing a server. Closing the connection does not flush the last event. A
server that writes `data: done\n` and hangs up has sent nothing at all, and the bug presents as "the
last message is missing sometimes".

The page's sandbox steps one stream through five chunk boundaries — the first cuts a field name in
half — showing the partial line held in the parser buffer and the events appearing only on blank
lines. That parser is the one test-model.ts checks against a real node:http server.

Source: WHATWG HTML — Server-Sent Events,
https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/server-sent-events.html

## 04. EventSource, reconnection, and what you get for free

    const es = new EventSource("/events");
    es.onmessage = (e) => { const ev = JSON.parse(e.data); handleEvent(ev); };
    es.addEventListener("task.completed", (e) => { /* only `event: task.completed` */ });

Free: parsing, dispatch by event type, and automatic reconnection. When the connection drops the
browser waits the reconnection time and reopens the request, announcing where it got to. The spec:
"The Last-Event-ID HTTP request header reports an EventSource object's last event ID string to the
server when the user agent is to reestablish the connection."

So resumption is a two-sided contract and the browser only holds up one side. It sends the header;
whether anything useful happens depends on your server reading it. A server that ignores
Last-Event-ID and replays from the top delivers duplicates forever, every time a laptop lid closes.

What EventSource will not do:
- Custom headers, including Authorization. Options: a cookie, a token in the query string (which
  lands in access logs), or moving to fetch + ReadableStream (§07). Most production SSE code ends up
  in the third bucket, and this is usually why.
- Anything but GET. No request body, so an endpoint needing a large input — a model prompt — cannot
  use EventSource at all.
- Give up. It reconnects indefinitely; closing it is your job, via es.close().

The other design: a server holding a small bounded buffer can hand every new connection the whole
buffer and let the client sort it out, which is what 4th-devs does for its agent dashboard
deliberately — the client re-renders from scratch and de-duplicates by id, so exact resumption never
has to be the server's job. A legitimate trade; the page's sandbox shows the cost of getting the
client half wrong, where the replayed buffer lands as duplicates.

## 05. The server side: where your events meet the socket

    res.writeHead(200, {
      'content-type': 'text/event-stream',
      'cache-control': 'no-cache',
      connection: 'keep-alive',
    })
    res.flushHeaders()
    for (const past of replay()) res.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify(past)}\n\n`)
    const unsubscribe = subscribe(event => res.write(`data: ${JSON.stringify(event)}\n\n`))

Source: 4th-devs, https://github.com/i-am-alice/4th-devs/blob/main/05_01_agent_graph/src/server.ts

The last line is the seam this page sits on. On its left, subscribe belongs to an in-process event
bus with no idea who is listening — that is event-driven architecture, and it has its own page:
https://pasekpasek.github.io/event-driven-architecture-worked-out/. On its right, res.write is one
socket belonging to one identified browser. Swap the right-hand side for a Kafka producer and the
left-hand side does not change. SSE is the transport; the bus is the architecture; that line is the
adapter.

The two lines that are not in the snippet:

    // 1. Keep-alive: a comment line, ignored by the parser, that keeps bytes flowing
    //    so idle proxies and load balancers don't reap the connection (§09).
    const ping = setInterval(() => res.write(': keep-alive\n\n'), 15_000)

    // 2. Cleanup: without this, every disconnect leaks a listener and a timer, and the
    //    bus keeps writing to a dead socket.
    req.on('close', () => { clearInterval(ping); unsubscribe(); })

The cleanup is not bookkeeping. A subscriber list that only grows is a memory leak and a slow CPU
leak — each dead connection still gets serialised into on every event — presenting as "the dashboard
gets slower the longer it's been up".

## 06. A model's tokens are an SSE stream

Set stream: true on an Anthropic Messages API call and the response body is exactly a
text/event-stream, with the same \n\n, the same event: and data: fields and the same buffering
problem. The difference is that the event types and payloads are documented rather than made up per
app.

Why models stream at all: a model produces its answer one token at a time, and a long answer takes
seconds to finish. Without streaming the user watches an empty box until the last token exists. With
streaming each piece of text goes out as its own event as soon as it's generated. The total time is
the same. What changes is how long until the first word shows up.

What is on the wire, one text fragment (⏎ = \n):

    event: content_block_delta⏎
    data: {"type":"content_block_delta","index":0,"delta":{"type":"text_delta","text":" cat"}}⏎
    ⏎

The client cuts on the blank line, runs JSON.parse on the data: line and appends delta.text to the
screen. That's the whole "typing" effect.

One turn is a fixed sequence: message_start (the message shell, empty content array), then per
content block content_block_start → repeated content_block_delta → content_block_stop, then
message_delta (carrying stop_reason) and message_stop. A ping event may appear between deltas as a
keep-alive with no content — the same job as the ": keep-alive" comment line in §05, promoted to a
typed event.

A tool call is a content block whose content_block_start has "type": "tool_use" and a partial,
growing set of arguments: each content_block_delta for that block carries an input_json_delta with a
partial_json string fragment, not a complete value. The fragments concatenate and are only guaranteed
parseable once content_block_stop closes the block.

That is fact 2 one level up the stack. The blank line told you a line-oriented unit was complete;
content_block_stop tells you a semantic unit is complete. Both exist because the alternative —
guessing from the absence of more bytes — cannot distinguish "not yet" from "never". A client that
runs JSON.parse on each fragment as it arrives is making exactly that guess, and will be wrong on
every tool call with more than one delta.

The page's sandbox feeds the raw bytes of a tool-call turn, quoted verbatim from Anthropic's
published streaming documentation (not captured from a live API call), through the same parser as
§03, one event at a time: raw bytes, the dispatched event, the text on screen, and the tool input
accumulating as a string that is not valid JSON until the block closes.

Source: https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/streaming

In a real app there are two streams, not one. The browser never calls the model API directly, because
that would ship your API key to every visitor:

    1  browser     -- POST /api/chat {messages} ------> your server
    2  your server -- POST /v1/messages + x-api-key --> model API
    3  model API   -- SSE: content_block_delta... ----> your server
    4  your server -- SSE: your own events -----------> browser

The simplest middle passes bytes through unchanged, since \n\n means the same thing on both hops:

    app.post("/api/chat", async (req, res) => {
      const upstream = new AbortController();
      res.on("close", () => upstream.abort());   // browser left -> stop paying for tokens
      const model = await fetch("https://api.anthropic.com/v1/messages", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          "x-api-key": process.env.ANTHROPIC_API_KEY,   // stays on the server
          "anthropic-version": "2023-06-01",
          "content-type": "application/json",
        },
        body: JSON.stringify({ model: "claude-opus-5", max_tokens: 1024, stream: true, messages: req.body.messages }),
        signal: upstream.signal,
      });
      res.writeHead(200, { "content-type": "text/event-stream", "cache-control": "no-cache" });
      res.flushHeaders();
      for await (const chunk of model.body) res.write(chunk);   // bytes in, bytes out
      res.end();
    });

In practice the middle usually parses the model's events, saves the answer, counts tokens and
re-emits only what the UI needs. A model stream can't be resumed: its events carry no id: field, so
there's no Last-Event-ID to send back. If the connection drops halfway through an answer, the answer
is gone; you send the request again or keep the partial text. §04's machinery only applies to the
stream your own server writes, and only if it buffers the generation and numbers its events.

## 07. Consuming a stream in TypeScript

§04 explained why real code often cannot use EventSource: no headers, no request body, GET only. The
replacement is fetch plus the response's ReadableStream.

    const res = await fetch("/api/chat", {           // your server (§06), never the model API directly
      method: "POST",                                 // EventSource cannot do this
      headers: { authorization: `Bearer ${sessionToken}` },  // nor this (your app's login)
      body: JSON.stringify({ messages }),
      signal: controller.signal,                      // nor cancellation
    });

    const reader = res.body!.getReader();
    const decoder = new TextDecoder();
    const parser = createSseParser();

    for (;;) {
      const { value, done } = await reader.read();
      if (done) break;
      for (const event of parser.push(decoder.decode(value, { stream: true }))) {
        if (event.event !== "content_block_delta") continue;
        const { delta } = JSON.parse(event.data);     // safe: the event is complete
        if (delta.type === "text_delta") output.textContent += delta.text;
      }
    }

parser.push only returns an event once its blank line has arrived, so JSON.parse never sees half a
line. It can still see half a tool call, which is why §06 accumulates partial_json.

Two buffers are in play and they are easy to confuse. The parser buffers a partial LINE until a
newline arrives (§03). The decoder buffers partial BYTES until a whole character arrives — that is
what { stream: true } buys. The Encoding standard: "The method can be invoked zero or more times with
options's stream set to true, and then once without options's stream (or set to false), to process a
fragmented input."

Drop the option and the code still works — on English text. UTF-8 encodes anything outside ASCII as
two to four bytes, and fact 1 says the chunk boundary can land anywhere, including between them. A
decoder told the input is complete does the only thing it can with half a character: replaces it with
U+FFFD. The bytes are gone; no later chunk repairs them.

The page's sandbox splits `data: {"t":"café ☕"}` at byte offsets that cut the three-byte ☕ in half
and decodes the same bytes both ways side by side: the naive decoder ends with three U+FFFD where one
character used to be, the streaming decoder with the text the server sent. A split that falls between
characters is harmless either way, which is exactly why the bug survives code review.

Cancellation is not optional. A streaming request the user navigated away from is still running,
still costing money if a model is on the other end, and still holding a connection. Use an
AbortController, pass its signal to fetch, call abort(), and treat AbortError as a normal exit rather
than a failure — otherwise every cancelled stream reports itself as a crash.

Source: WHATWG Encoding, https://encoding.spec.whatwg.org/#dom-textdecoder-decode

## 08. SSE, WebSocket, long-polling: picking one

- SSE — a GET that never finishes, in a text format. One direction, server to client. Reconnection
  and resumption are in the spec. Pick it when the data flows one way: notifications, progress, logs,
  model tokens. It is ordinary HTTP, so proxies, auth, compression and observability already work.
- WebSocket — a protocol upgrade to a persistent, bidirectional, framed connection, no longer HTTP
  after the handshake. Pick it when the client genuinely sends a lot, continuously: typing
  indicators, multiplayer, collaborative editing. You inherit its infrastructure: your own
  heartbeats, your own reconnect-and-resume, and middleboxes that understand none of it.
- Long-polling — a request the server holds until it has something, then answers, and the client
  immediately asks again. Correct, simple, and it pays a full round-trip per message.

The one genuine constraint is connection count, and it is a browser limit rather than a protocol one.
MDN: "When not used over HTTP/2, SSE suffers from a limitation to the maximum number of open
connections, which can be especially painful when opening multiple tabs, as the limit is per browser
and is set to a very low number (6)." Over HTTP/2 the ceiling is negotiated and "defaults to 100".

"But I need to send data back" is usually not an argument: the client can make ordinary HTTP requests
whenever it likes. A stream down and normal POSTs up is a perfectly good bidirectional system, and it
is how every streaming model API on the market works. Reach for WebSocket when the upward traffic is
continuous, not merely present.

Source: https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events/Using_server-sent_events

## 09. What goes wrong

- A buffering proxy. The most common cause. nginx buffers proxied responses by default — right for
  ordinary responses, fatal for this one. Fix with proxy_buffering off, or send X-Accel-Buffering: no
  so the decision travels with the response rather than living in someone else's config file.
- Compression without flushing. A gzip layer waiting for a full window does what the proxy did, one
  layer lower. Disable compression for text/event-stream or flush per write.
- Idle timeouts. Load balancers reap connections with no bytes on them, commonly after 60 seconds. If
  your stream can be quiet longer than that, §05's keep-alive comment is what keeps you connected.
- No cleanup on disconnect. Without req.on('close', ...) the subscriber list grows forever and every
  event is serialised for sockets nobody is reading.
- Assuming one write is one message. Fact 1. It works until a payload gets big or a proxy coalesces.
- Ignoring backpressure. res.write() returns false when the kernel buffer is full; a producer that
  keeps writing grows an unbounded queue in process memory, so a slow client becomes your memory
  problem. That is the event loop's business: https://pasekpasek.github.io/event-loop-worked-out/

Diagnostic: run curl -N against the endpoint directly, then through your proxy. If events appear live
in the first and arrive in a clump in the second, nothing in your application code is wrong.

## 10. The whole page in rules, and scope

1. One write() is not one read(). Anything that assumes otherwise is correct on localhost and wrong
   in production.
2. Every stream needs a framing rule, because "no more bytes yet" and "no more bytes ever" look
   identical. SSE's is a blank line, which on the wire is just \n\n: one \n ends a field, the
   second ends the event. A model turn's is content_block_stop.
3. Closing the connection does not dispatch the last event. It needs its blank line, and the spec
   says so in as many words.
4. Streaming over HTTP is not a hack: chunked transfer coding exists to carry "content streams of
   unknown size". Remember flushHeaders().
5. Resumption is a two-sided contract. The browser sends Last-Event-ID; if your server ignores it,
   every reconnect replays duplicates. Replaying a bounded buffer instead is valid, but only with a
   client that de-duplicates.
6. EventSource cannot set headers, cannot POST, and never gives up. Real code usually ends up on
   fetch + ReadableStream for the first of those reasons.
7. Decode with { stream: true }. A multi-byte character split across chunks becomes U+FFFD
   permanently, and it only happens to text you did not test with.
8. Cancel with AbortController, and treat AbortError as a normal exit.
9. A model's reply streams to your server, and your server streams to the browser. The API key
   never leaves the server, and a dropped model stream can't be resumed. Only the stream you write
   yourself can carry id:s.
10. Send keep-alive comments and clean up on close. One keeps proxies from reaping you; the other
    keeps you from leaking a listener per disconnect.
11. If it works with curl -N and not through the proxy, it is the proxy. Over HTTP/1.1 you also get
    six connections per browser, total.

Left out, on purpose:

- The architecture on the other side of the seam. What produces the events, who else consumes them,
  what a broker guarantees about delivery and ordering — a different question from how bytes cross a
  socket, with its own page:
  https://pasekpasek.github.io/event-driven-architecture-worked-out/
  §05's subscribe(event => res.write(event)) is the seam between the two.
- WebSocket in earnest. Named and compared in §08, not built. Frames, ping/pong, subprotocols and
  scaling a stateful connection layer are a page of their own.
- gRPC streaming and HTTP/2 server push. Both real, both a different ecosystem, and neither is what a
  browser talking to a JSON API reaches for.

## About this page's models

Four of this page's models are backed by running code, checked by test-model.ts (15 checks):

- The SSE parser is checked against a real node:http server, including an event deliberately split
  across two TCP-level writes, over a real fetch + ReadableStream client.
- The WHATWG dispatch rules are executed: a stream ending without a blank line dispatches nothing, an
  incomplete line is held in the buffer rather than guessed at, and a comment line dispatches nothing.
- The UTF-8 boundary is checked against the real TextDecoder: that the fixture genuinely cuts the
  three-byte ☕ in half, that { stream: true } reassembles it exactly, that omitting the option
  replaces it with U+FFFD permanently, and that a clean split is harmless either way.
- The two resumption designs are checked: Last-Event-ID sends exactly what was missed, replay without
  client de-duplication produces duplicates, replay with it ends up identical to resuming by id, and
  a client with no Last-Event-ID gets the whole buffer rather than nothing.

The RFC 9112, WHATWG HTML, WHATWG Encoding and MDN statements are quoted from those documents, not
reproduced locally. The §06 streaming fixture is quoted from Anthropic's own published documentation,
not captured from a live API call.

Run the harness: node test-model.ts
